patches.originalSourceStem: A sample contains $2\times 10^{11}$ particles, each of mass $3\times 10^{-7}$ g. A filter removes $25\%$ of the total mass. The remainder occupies $1.5\times 10^{2}$ cm$^3$. Find its density in g/cm$^3$ in standard form.

replacement.stem: A hypothetical material contains $2\times 10^{11}$ particles, each of mass $3\times 10^{-10}$ g. A filter removes $25\%$ of the total mass. The remainder occupies $1.5\times 10^{2}$ cm$^3$. Find its density in g/cm$^3$ in standard form.

options.misconception: Divide the retained 45 g by 15 cm³ instead of 150 cm³ (volume scale ×10 error): 3 g/cm³.
Keep 50% of the starting 60 g rather than 75%: 30/150=0.2 g/cm³.
Drop the 1.5 coefficient in 1.5×10² cm³, divide 45 g by 100 cm³: 0.45 g/cm³.
Ignore filtering and use the full 60 g: 60/150=0.4 g/cm³.

workedSolutionSteps: Total mass $=(2\times 10^{11})(3\times 10^{-10})=6\times10^{1}$ g. After removing $25\%$, retain $75\%$: $0.75\times60=45$ g.

originalWorkedSolutionSteps: Collect $x$: $(1z-4)x=5-6z$, then replace $z=y-1$ to obtain $x=- \frac{6 y - 11}{y - 5}$.

workedSolutionSteps: Domain: the original denominator requires $x\ne-6$. Put $z=y-1$ and multiply both sides by $x+6$: $z(x+6)=4x+5$.
Collect $x$: $(z-4)x=5-6z$. Since $z=4$ would give the impossible statement $24=5$, $y\ne5$. Thus $x=\dfrac{11-6y}{y-5}=-\dfrac{6y-11}{y-5}$.
